misconceptions.statement: The money I pay with UPI is stored inside the UPI app, like a wallet.
misconceptions.why: Apps show balances and payment history, so students think the app holds the money.
misconceptions.fix: The money stays in your bank account. UPI sends it directly from your bank to the receiver's bank.

probe.question: If your UPI app is deleted from your phone, what happens to the money in your account?
probe.wrong_answer: The money is lost because it was kept inside the app.

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible app holds the actual thing

misconceptions.statement: UPI is a private company's app, like PhonePe or Google Pay.
misconceptions.why: Students only ever see the brand-name apps and never the system behind them.
misconceptions.fix: UPI is a payment system built by NPCI, supported by RBI. PhonePe, Google Pay, BHIM and others are apps that connect to it.

probe.question: Who owns UPI?
probe.wrong_answer: Google, because Google Pay is the main UPI app.

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible brand is the whole system

misconceptions.statement: UPI can only be used on a smartphone with internet.
misconceptions.why: Most students see UPI only through smartphone apps.
misconceptions.fix: UPI can also work on basic phones through services like *99# and UPI 123PAY, without a smartphone app.

probe.question: Can a person with a basic keypad phone make a UPI payment?
probe.wrong_answer: No, UPI needs a smartphone and internet.

misconceptions.root_belief: what I commonly see is the only way

misconceptions.statement: If someone knows my UPI ID, they can take money out of my account.
misconceptions.why: Students treat every detail of the account as a password.
misconceptions.fix: A UPI ID is like an address for receiving money. Taking money out needs your UPI PIN, so sharing the ID is safe.

probe.question: You give your UPI ID to a friend so they can pay you back. Is it dangerous?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they can now take money from my account.

misconceptions.root_belief: knowing information means having access

misconceptions.statement: The UPI PIN is the same as my ATM card PIN or phone lock code.
misconceptions.why: All three are short numeric codes and are used for similar-sounding security.
misconceptions.fix: The UPI PIN is set separately for UPI. It can be different from the ATM PIN and the phone lock code, and must be kept secret like them.

probe.question: You forgot your UPI PIN. Can you use your phone lock code instead?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the UPI PIN is the same as the phone lock code.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-looking things are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: A bank or UPI app employee may sometimes need my PIN to fix a problem.
misconceptions.why: Students believe officials need complete access to help them.
misconceptions.fix: No bank or UPI app staff will ever ask for your PIN. Anyone who asks for it is a fraudster.

probe.question: A caller says they are from your bank and need your UPI PIN to reverse a failed payment. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Give the PIN, since they are from the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: an official helper needs full access
misconceptions.source_hint: RBI and NPCI public awareness campaigns on digital fraud; surveys of fraud victims

misconceptions.statement: An OTP is safe to tell someone if they say they are from my bank.
misconceptions.why: Students trust anyone who claims authority and think OTPs are harmless numbers.
misconceptions.fix: An OTP is meant only for you. Never share it with anyone, including people who say they are from the bank.

probe.question: A caller from 'the bank' asks for the OTP you just received to cancel a wrong payment. Should you tell it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are from the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: people claiming authority can be trusted
misconceptions.source_hint: RBI public awareness material on OTP fraud; studies of vishing victims

misconceptions.statement: A caller who knows my name and bank details must be genuine.
misconceptions.why: Students think only a real bank could know such personal details.
misconceptions.fix: Fraudsters collect names and details from leaks and social media. Knowing your details does not prove a caller is genuine.

probe.question: A caller says your name, bank and last four account digits and asks for your OTP. Is the caller real?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they know my details so they must be from the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: knowing personal details proves identity
misconceptions.source_hint: cyber-safety awareness research on social engineering and impersonation scams

misconceptions.statement: Installing an app a helpful caller asks for is harmless as long as I do not say my PIN.
misconceptions.why: Students think a secret is only given away by saying it aloud.
misconceptions.fix: Screen-sharing or remote-access apps let a stranger watch your screen and see your PIN and OTP. Never install them on a stranger's advice.

probe.question: A caller asks you to install a screen-sharing app 'to fix your refund' but says not to tell the PIN. Is it safe?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since I am not telling the PIN.

misconceptions.root_belief: a secret is only lost if I say it

misconceptions.statement: The OTP that arrives on my phone is my UPI PIN.
misconceptions.why: Both are secret numeric codes used for approving money matters.
misconceptions.fix: A PIN is a fixed secret you create and remember. An OTP is a new code sent for one use only and expires quickly.

probe.question: Is your UPI PIN the number that comes by SMS each time?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the SMS number is the PIN.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar-looking things are the same thing

misconceptions.statement: To receive money by UPI I must enter my PIN.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the sending steps and assume every money step needs a PIN.
misconceptions.fix: A PIN is needed only to send money. Receiving money never needs your PIN, so anyone asking for it to 'send you money' is cheating.

probe.question: A buyer says: 'Enter your PIN to receive my payment.' What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Enter the PIN because receiving needs it.

misconceptions.root_belief: every step of a process needs the same checks
misconceptions.source_hint: RBI and NPCI awareness advisories on receive-money and marketplace scams

misconceptions.statement: Scanning a QR code sent by a buyer will make money come into my account.
misconceptions.why: Students think scanning always means taking and not giving.
misconceptions.fix: Scanning a QR code and entering a PIN sends money out of your account. You never need to scan anything to receive money.

probe.question: A buyer sends you a QR code to scan so they can pay you. What happens when you scan and enter your PIN?
probe.wrong_answer: I receive the money.

misconceptions.root_belief: the direction of an action is always inward
misconceptions.source_hint: NPCI and RBI fraud awareness advisories on QR code scams

misconceptions.statement: Only the amount matters when paying a QR code; the name shown does not.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the number they type and skip the payee details.
misconceptions.fix: Always read the payee name on the confirmation screen. A wrong name may mean you are paying a stranger.

probe.question: You scan a shop's QR but the name shown is a person you don't know. What should you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Pay anyway, since the amount is correct.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the numbers matter

misconceptions.statement: A printed QR code at a shop is always genuine.
misconceptions.why: Students trust anything that looks official and printed.
misconceptions.fix: Fraudsters can paste fake QR codes over real ones. Check the payee name shown after scanning.

probe.question: A QR sticker is pasted at a roadside stall. Is it safe to pay without checking?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a printed QR is always genuine.

misconceptions.root_belief: looking official means genuine

misconceptions.statement: Approving a collect request means I will receive money.
misconceptions.why: The word 'accept' sounds like receiving something.
misconceptions.fix: A collect request asks you to pay. Approving it and entering your PIN sends money out of your account.

probe.question: You get a collect request from a stranger. If you approve it, who gets the money?
probe.wrong_answer: I get the money.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: NPCI and RBI awareness advisories on collect request fraud

misconceptions.statement: A collect request mentioning a prize or refund is safe to approve.
misconceptions.why: Students believe a good-sounding message means a good purpose.
misconceptions.fix: Scammers use words like refund, cashback or prize to trick you. Decline any collect request you did not expect.

probe.question: A collect request says 'Cashback Rs 500, approve to claim'. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Approve it to get the cashback.

misconceptions.root_belief: a nice message means a nice intention

misconceptions.statement: There is no limit on how much money can be sent by UPI in a day.
misconceptions.why: Digital payments feel unlimited because no physical cash is handled.
misconceptions.fix: UPI has limits, usually Rs 1 lakh a day per account for most payments. Banks and apps may set lower limits.

probe.question: Can you send Rs 5 lakh to a friend through UPI in one day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UPI has no limit.

misconceptions.root_belief: digital things have no limits

misconceptions.statement: Using two different UPI apps gives me a separate daily limit on each.
misconceptions.why: Students think each app keeps its own count.
misconceptions.fix: Limits are set on the bank account, so using more apps does not add more limit for the same account.

probe.question: Your limit is Rs 1 lakh a day. Can you send Rs 1 lakh from one app and Rs 1 lakh from another for the same account?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, each app has its own limit.

misconceptions.root_belief: separate containers have separate limits

misconceptions.statement: Every UPI payment costs the sender a fee.
misconceptions.why: Students assume digital services always charge, like card or transfer fees.
misconceptions.fix: Ordinary UPI payments between people and to shops are free for users.

probe.question: Do you pay a fee to send Rs 100 to a friend by UPI?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, UPI always charges a fee.

misconceptions.root_belief: every service must charge a fee

misconceptions.statement: Once money is sent through UPI to a fraudster, nothing can be done.
misconceptions.why: Students think digital payments cannot be undone.
misconceptions.fix: Report immediately to your bank and call 1930 or use cybercrime.gov.in. Quick reporting can help freeze the money.

probe.question: You were cheated of Rs 2000 by UPI. What is the point of reporting?
probe.wrong_answer: No point, money sent is gone forever.

misconceptions.root_belief: what is done digitally cannot be undone

misconceptions.statement: I should wait a few days before reporting a UPI fraud to be sure.
misconceptions.why: Students feel unsure and hope the money may return.
misconceptions.fix: Report within minutes or hours. Faster reporting gives a better chance to stop the money from being withdrawn.

probe.question: You notice a fraud payment. When should you report it?
probe.wrong_answer: After a few days when I am sure.

misconceptions.root_belief: waiting is harmless
